extracted.intended_audience: members, ministers, and sympathizers of the Reformed Presbyterian Church; readers of the Presbytery's Testimony
extracted.subtask_description: A mid-19th-century Presbytery testimony setting out doctrinal, moral, and procedural standards for ministers and members: what doctrines to accept, what practices to reject, duties of Christians and the church, and explicit terms for ministerial and Christian communion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oaths and vows as religious worship
rubrics_metrics.description: Oaths and vows are part of religious worship, warranted in Scripture under the New Testament, lawful when both the matter and manner are lawful, and once engaged in must not be violated because of God's name interposed in them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only those oaths lawful in matter and manner are warrantable; the right to administer oaths is competent only to those vested with authority agreeable to Scripture. Christians may solemnly bind themselves by oath to maintain and defend righteous rulers (swearing allegiance/fidelity only to lawful rulers). The Presbytery disapproves refusing allegiance to lawful authority, but testifies against oaths of allegiance to an Erastian Prelatical government. They reject profane practices (laying hand on and kissing the gospels) as a profanation, condemn sinful/common swearing and unnecessary commercial/state oaths, and explicitly condemn Masonic oaths as ungodly and superstitious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lawfulness and binding nature of public covenanting
rubrics_metrics.description: Solemn public covenanting with God in Christ is a duty warranted in Old and New Testament examples, applicable to individuals, churches, and nations; lawful covenants once entered and lawful in matter are sacred and inviolably binding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The National Covenant of Scotland and the Solemn League and Covenant are held to be of divine authority and perpetual moral obligation (including posterity). The Presbytery testifies against any principle or practice that undermines the lawfulness or moral obligation of national covenanting under the New Testament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adherence to historic Reformation standards (confessions and formularies)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Presbytery adheres to the Westminster Confession of Faith (as approved 1647), the larger and shorter Catechisms, the Form of Church Government, Directory for Worship, and Books of Discipline as agreeable to Scripture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These documents and steps of reformation are to be approved and adhered to; the Presbytery rejects corrupt glosses or reinterpretations inconsistent with the original reformed understanding. The Form of Government and Directory adopted by the Church of Scotland in the Second Reformation is presented as the most perfect model attained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper interpretation of Confessional article (rejection of corrupt gloss)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Presbytery rejects a corrupt sense imposed upon the fourth article of chapter 23 of the Confession that would allow a reformed people to lawfully acknowledge an infidel or person of a different religion as their civil ruler simply because the people had embraced true religion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They interpret that article as principally relating to peoples emerging from paganism/popery before civil sanction of the true religion, not as a license to accept an infidel ruler in a fully reformed nation; use apostolic precedent (1 Cor. vii; 2 Cor. vi) to limit the article's application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Faithfulness and completeness of public testimonies
rubrics_metrics.description: Public testimonies and declarations must be faithful, comprehensive vindications of the covenanted cause; partiality or unfaithfulness in published testimonies (left- or right-leaning extremes) is condemned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject testimonies that are partial, unfaithful, or amount to a burial of important attainments in reformation (the Presbytery specifically rejects the Associate Presbytery's testimony and certain writings claimed as 'testimonies' but considered spurious or enthusiastic). Testimonies should align with Scripture and historic reformation principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial Declaration 1 — view of human agency and divine decree
rubrics_metrics.description: Man is a free agent, not conscious of restraint in his volitions by God's immutable decree; it is not possible to avoid fulfilling that decree; nevertheless the law of God (not his decree) is the rule of man's conduct and the standard of final judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affirms a doctrinal balance: human voluntary agency coexists with divine decree, while ethical responsibility rests on God's law as the normative standard for conduct and judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial Declaration 2 — duty toward the church
rubrics_metrics.description: It is the duty of a Christian to pray for the church of Christ, to inquire diligently into her scriptural character, and to seek covenant blessings in her communion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Personal and communal practices (prayer, careful discernment, seeking covenantal blessing) are incumbent duties for Christians in relation to the church.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial Declaration 3 — right and duty to testify and separate
rubrics_metrics.description: If the majority violate the terms on which church members were united, it is lawful for the minority to testify against the defection and to walk by the rule of their former attainments; if a body assuming to be the Church imposes sinful terms of communion, is anti-scriptural in constitution, or corrupt in administration and reformation attempts fail, Christians have a duty to separate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives procedural and moral justification for separation and minority testimony: separation is warranted where constitutional or administrative corruption persists and reformation proves ineffectual (scriptural reference: Rev. xviii, 'Come out of her, my people').

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial Declaration 4 — prohibitions on civic and ecclesiastical participation
rubrics_metrics.description: No member of the Reformed Presbyterian Church can, without contracting guilt in the present state of society, take the oath of allegiance to the government of the United States, hold civil office, exercise the elective franchise (vote), act as a juror, or hold communion in other ecclesiastical bodies by 'occasional hearing'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an explicit behavioral/disciplinary rule restricting members' civic participation and inter-ecclesiastical practices on conscientious and doctrinal grounds (references: Rev. xi, 1-3).

rubrics_metrics.name: Term 1 — Scripture as sole infallible rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledgement that the Old and New Testaments are the Word of God and the alone infallible rule of faith and practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Membership and ministerial communion require explicit acceptance of biblical authority as the ultimate and sole infallible standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Term 2 — conformity to the Westminster system
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledgement that the whole doctrine of the Westminster Confession of Faith and the larger and shorter Catechisms are agreeable to and founded upon the Scriptures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Members/ministers must accept the Westminster doctrinal standards as scriptural and binding in principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Term 3 — divine right of Presbyterian government
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledgement that Presbyterian church government is of divine right and unalterable; the best model is the Form of Government and Directory for Worship as adopted by the Church of Scotland in the Second Reformation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reaffirms polity as doctrinal: acceptance of Presbyterian governance (its form and Directory) is a condition of communion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Term 4 — obligation of public social covenanting
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledgement that public, social covenanting is an ordinance of God, obligatory on churches and nations under the New Testament; the National Covenant of Scotland and the Solemn League and Covenant are exemplifications and are of perpetual obligation (including acknowledgment of Auchensaugh 1712 renovations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Membership requires acceptance of the practice and ongoing moral obligation of national and ecclesiastical covenanting as a biblical ordinance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Term 5 — approbation of historic martyrs and judicial acts
rubrics_metrics.description: Approves the faithful contendings of martyrs against paganism, popery, prelacy, malignancy, sectarianism, and immoral civil constitutions (Erastian tolerations and persecutions); endorses the Judicial Act, Declaration and Testimony (1761) and Historical/Declaratory Supplements (Reformed Church in North America, 1850) as exemplary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Members should honor and uphold the historical testimonies and judicial acts that defended reformation principles, seeing these as models for present fidelity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Term 6 — practical holiness in conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Practically adorning the doctrine of God our Savior by walking in all his commandments and ordinances blamelessly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Membership implies not merely doctrinal assent but practical obedience and blameless living according to Christian commandments and ordinances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Testimony against civil and ecclesiastical support for Popery and Erastianism
rubrics_metrics.description: The Presbytery testifies against governmental measures and ecclesiastical practices that support or tolerate Popery (Catholicism) and Erastian supremacy—opposing legal toleration, civil privileges, and alliances perceived to advance Popery or undermine Protestant reformation principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly condemns laws or policies granting civil/religious privileges to Catholics (e.g., Quebec Act), alliances that aid Papal interests (military/political alliances), state fasts imposed by an Erastian supremacy, and ministers who sanction such measures instead of warning the people.
